claims.evidence: The abstract reports correlation between chromatin accessibility and gene expression.

claims.claim: Four Cre lines crossed to the Ai14 reporter line were used to access layer-specific glutamatergic cells in the mouse visual cortex.
claims.source: To access layer-specific glutamatergic cells in the mouse visual cortex, we used four previously characterized Cre lines crossed to the Ai14 reporter line (Madisen et al., 2010), which expresses tdTomato (tdT) after Cre-mediated recombination (Figure 1A,B).
claims.evidence: The methods section describes the genetic tools used, and Figure 1 shows the experimental design.

claims.claim: Each Cre line used contains at least two closely related cell types based on scRNA-seq.
claims.source: Although these lines mostly label cells in specific cortical layers, we note that each contains at least two closely related cell types based on scRNA-seq (Figure 1C, Tasic et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1C and a previous publication.

claims.claim: Gad2-IRES-Cre was used to profile GABAergic cell types.
claims.source: As a control, we profiled GABAergic cell types using Gad2-IRES-Cre.
claims.evidence: The methods section describes the genetic tool used for GABAergic cells.

claims.claim: The study restricted analysis to eight week-old male mice and cells microdissected only from the visual cortex to minimize heterogeneity.
claims.source: We tried to minimize other potential sources of heterogeneity that may be caused by age, sex, or cortical region by restricting our analysis to eight week-old male mice, and cells microdissected only from the visual cortex (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: The methods section describes the experimental design to control for variables.

claims.claim: Triplicates of 500 cell populations were collected from each Cre line and from at least two mice per line.
claims.source: We collected triplicates of 500 cell populations from each Cre line and from at least two mice per line.
claims.evidence: The methods section describes the sample collection strategy.

claims.claim: Each ATAC-seq sample showed fragment size patterns characteristic of open chromatin and mono-, di-, and tri-nucleosomal fragments.
claims.source: Each sample showed fragment size patterns characteristic of open chromatin and mono-, di-, and tri-nucleosomal fragments (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), as well as a clear accessibility footprint around motifs for the ubiquitously-expressed transcription factor ATF2 throughout the genome (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The text describes quality control metrics and references figures showing the data.

claims.claim: Each ATAC-seq sample showed a clear accessibility footprint around motifs for the ubiquitously-expressed transcription factor ATF2 throughout the genome.
claims.source: Each sample showed fragment size patterns characteristic of open chromatin and mono-, di-, and tri-nucleosomal fragments (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), as well as a clear accessibility footprint around motifs for the ubiquitously-expressed transcription factor ATF2 throughout the genome (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The text describes quality control metrics and references figures showing the data.

claims.claim: Data obtained from Tn5 tagmentation of purified genomic DNA from 500 mES cells do not display characteristic ATAC-seq signatures.
claims.source: In comparison, data obtained from Tn5 tagmentation of purified genomic DNA from 500 mES cells do not display these characteristic signatures (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The text describes negative control results and references figures showing the data.

claims.claim: The distribution of accessible sites revealed six peak populations: distal upstream (> 2 kb upstream of TSS), upstream (< 2 kb upstream, > 200 bp upstream), proximal upstream (< 200 bp from TSS), proximal downstream (< 200 bp), downstream (200 bp to 2 kb), and distal downstream (> 2 kb).
claims.source: The distribution of accessible sites revealed six peak populations: distal upstream (> 2 kb upstream of TSS; abbreviated −3), upstream (< 2 kb upstream, > 200 bp upstream; −2), proximal upstream (< 200 bp from TSS; −1), proximal downstream (< 200 bp; +1), downstream (200 bp to 2 kb; +2), and distal downstream (> 2 kb; +3).
claims.evidence: The text describes the classification of peaks based on their position relative to TSS.

claims.claim: Very similar distributions of peak locations were found in different cell classes.
claims.source: We found very similar distributions of peak locations in different cell classes, and found our distribution to be very similar to the one derived from previously published neuronal ATAC-seq data (Camk2a-Cre, [Mo et al., 2015]), Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The text describes comparison of peak distributions across cell classes and references figures.

claims.claim: The peak distribution in this study is very similar to the one derived from previously published neuronal ATAC-seq data (Camk2a-Cre, Mo et al., 2015).
claims.source: We found very similar distributions of peak locations in different cell classes, and found our distribution to be very similar to the one derived from previously published neuronal ATAC-seq data (Camk2a-Cre, [Mo et al., 2015]), Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The text describes comparison to previously published data and references figures.

claims.claim: Data derived from 500 cells per sample compare well with ATAC-seq data obtained from more than 1 million Camk2a-Cre-labeled nuclei per sample.

claims.evidence: The text describes comparison to previously published data with different input cell numbers.

claims.claim: Most proximal peaks overlapped with promoter marks in all cell classes including mES cells, suggesting that these are indeed promoters.
claims.source: We found that most proximal peaks overlapped with promoter marks in all cell classes including mES cells, suggesting that these are indeed promoters, and that promoter accessibility is frequently not cell class-specific.
claims.evidence: The text describes overlap analysis with ChIP-seq data and draws inference about peak function.

claims.claim: Promoter accessibility is frequently not cell class-specific.
claims.source: We found that most proximal peaks overlapped with promoter marks in all cell classes including mES cells, suggesting that these are indeed promoters, and that promoter accessibility is frequently not cell class-specific.
claims.evidence: The text describes overlap analysis with ChIP-seq data and draws inference about promoter accessibility.

claims.claim: Distal glutamatergic peaks more frequently overlapped with enhancer marks than distal peaks from interneuron cell classes.
claims.source: In contrast, distal peaks had stronger class-specific biases, as distal glutamatergic peaks more frequently overlapped with enhancer marks than distal peaks from interneuron cell classes (Mo et al., 2015).

claims.claim: ATAC-seq peaks from GABAergic and mES cells more frequently overlapped with polycomb-repressed regions from Camk2a-Cre-labeled glutamatergic cells.

claims.claim: Enhancer accessibility corresponds to specific cell classes, whereas many promoters may have similar accessibility across all classes.
claims.source: In summary, these results suggest that enhancer accessibility corresponds to specific cell classes, whereas many promoters may have similar accessibility across all classes.
claims.evidence: The text summarizes findings from overlap analysis with ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: ATAC-seq peak sets obtained from replicates of each cell class were most strongly correlated with each other.

claims.claim: Peak sets from cell classes clustered according to previous transcriptomic findings: GABAergic cells differed strongly from glutamatergic cell classes, and layer six was most distinct among glutamatergic cell classes.

claims.claim: Distal sites more cleanly delineated cell classes than proximal sites when clustering was performed separately.
claims.source: When clustering was performed separately on TSS-proximal and TSS-distal peaks, we found that distal sites more cleanly delineated cell classes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), as has been shown previously for hematopoeietic cell types (Corces et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Hierarchical clustering of differentially accessible peaks showed diverse combinatorial accessibility patterns between different neuronal classes.

claims.claim: Examination of accessibility near known marker genes corresponded with expected class-specific chromatin state.

claims.claim: Neuron-derived datasets were most similar to Whole Brain and Telencephalon tissue-derived DNase-seq data.

claims.claim: GABAergic datasets clustered with GABAergic whole cortex data.

claims.claim: Glutamatergic datasets clustered with the previously-published Camk2a-Cre datasets.

claims.claim: 83–94% of differentially accessible peaks, which were associated with differentially expressed genes, were positively correlated with gene expression.
claims.source: We found that overall peak accessibility corresponded to differential gene expression (Figure 4A): 83–94% of differentially accessible peaks, which were associated with differentially expressed genes, were positively correlated with gene expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The text reports quantitative results from correlation analysis and references figures.

claims.claim: Genes that are more highly expressed in GABAergic cells than in L4 cells, including Gad1, Slc6a1, and Dlx5, display prominent peaks of chromatin accessibility in GABAergic cells and not in L4 cells.
claims.source: For example, genes that are more highly expressed in GABAergic cells than in L4 cells, including Gad1, Slc6a1, and Dlx5, display prominent peaks of chromatin accessibility in GABAergic cells and not in L4 cells.

claims.claim: Slc17a7, Bdnf, and Nrn1, which are more highly expressed in L4 than in GABAergic cells, are associated with more accessible chromatin peaks specifically in L4 cells.

claims.evidence: The text describes specific examples of correlation between gene expression and chromatin accessibility and references a figure.

claims.claim: Calb1, Pou3f2, and Rorb are expressed in L4.

claims.claim: Bcl11b, Nfia, and Nos1ap are expressed in L6.

results.result: The study used four layer-specific Cre lines crossed to Ai14 reporter and Gad2-IRES-Cre for GABAergic cells to perform ATAC-seq on 500-cell populations from 8-week-old male mouse visual cortex. Each Cre line labels at least two closely related cell types based on scRNA-seq, and triplicates were collected from at least two mice per line.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C17-C21 describe the experimental design and methodology. The approach is clearly documented with appropriate controls (age, sex, cortical region), adequate replication (triplicates, multiple mice), and acknowledgment of cell type heterogeneity within each Cre line. The methodology is sound and well-justified.

results.result: ATAC-seq samples showed characteristic signatures of open chromatin including nucleosomal fragment patterns and ATF2 footprinting, while genomic DNA controls lacked these signatures.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 describe quality control metrics for ATAC-seq. The presence of expected signatures (nucleosomal patterns, TF footprints) in experimental samples and their absence in negative controls (purified genomic DNA) demonstrates technical validity of the assay. These are standard QC metrics for ATAC-seq.

results.result: The study identified a large number of accessible sites with six distinct peak populations based on distance to TSS. Peak distributions were similar across cell classes and comparable to previously published neuronal ATAC-seq data, despite using only 500 cells per sample versus >1 million nuclei in prior work.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C25-C28 describe peak identification and validation. The classification scheme is clearly defined, distributions are consistent across replicates and cell classes, and comparison to published data (Mo et al., 2015) validates the approach. The demonstration that 500-cell samples yield comparable results to million-cell datasets is an important technical validation.

results.result: Proximal peaks overlapped with promoter marks across all cell classes suggesting promoter accessibility is not cell-type specific, while distal peaks showed cell class-specific patterns with glutamatergic peaks enriched for enhancer marks and GABAergic/mES peaks enriched for polycomb-repressed regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 describe functional annotation of peaks through ChIP-seq overlap analysis. The findings are internally consistent and biologically plausible: promoters show broad accessibility while enhancers show cell-type specificity. The use of published ChIP-seq data (Mo et al., 2015) for validation is appropriate, though limited to Camk2a-Cre cells.

results.result: Hierarchical clustering showed that ATAC-seq replicates clustered together, cell classes clustered according to transcriptomic relationships (GABAergic distinct from glutamatergic; L6 most distinct among glutamatergic), and distal sites better delineated cell classes than proximal sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 describe clustering analysis results. The findings are well-supported: technical replicates cluster together (good reproducibility), biological relationships match transcriptomic data (Tasic et al., 2016), and distal vs. proximal differences align with known enhancer vs. promoter biology. The consistency with prior transcriptomic work strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: Differentially accessible peaks showed diverse combinatorial patterns across cell classes, accessibility near marker genes matched expected cell-class specificity, and the datasets clustered appropriately with published ENCODE and cortical ATAC-seq data.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C42 describe validation of differential accessibility patterns. The consistency between chromatin accessibility and known marker gene expression (C38), appropriate clustering with external datasets (C39-C42), and diverse combinatorial patterns (C37) all support the validity of the differential accessibility analysis. Multiple independent validations strengthen confidence.

results.result: Layer-specific accessible sites are significantly associated with layer-specific gene expression, with 83-94% of differentially accessible peaks positively correlated with gene expression of associated genes. Specific examples include GABAergic markers (Gad1, Slc6a1, Dlx5) and layer-specific markers (Calb1, Pou3f2, Rorb in L4; Bcl11b, Nfia, Nos1ap in L6), while 6-13% show negative correlation.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C16, C43-C48 establish correlation between chromatin accessibility and gene expression. The high percentage of positive correlations (83-94%) is quantitatively reported with statistical support. Specific examples validate the general pattern. The acknowledgment of negatively correlated peaks (6-13%) and discussion of potential mechanisms (repressor binding, misassignment) demonstrates appropriate scientific rigor. However, correlation does not establish causation.

results.result: K-means clustering identified peak and gene expression modules with layer-specific patterns. Each peak module was significantly enriched for genes in similarly patterned expression modules, including associations between non-identical but related patterns (e.g., Lower+ peaks with L6-only genes).
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 describe module analysis results. The statistical significance of peak-gene module associations is reported, and the identification of both matching and related patterns is biologically plausible. The methodology (k-means clustering with defined seed centroids) is described in detail in the methods, though the choice of 8 modules appears somewhat arbitrary.

results.result: Motif enrichment analysis identified layer-specific transcription factor binding motifs: L2/3 enriched for CUX, EGR1, FOXP, MEF2, POU3F, and RFX; L4 for RORB and NEUROD; L4 and L5 for FOS; and L6 for CUX, MEIS, NFIA and TBR1.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 report motif enrichment results from AME analysis. The findings are clearly stated and specific. However, the analysis is limited by the JASPAR database completeness (acknowledged by authors), and the biological significance depends on whether the corresponding TFs are expressed in the appropriate layers (addressed in C55-C60).

results.result: For most differentially enriched motifs, corresponding TF family members showed correlated or anticorrelated gene expression. Examples include positive correlations (ROR motifs with Rorb in L4, RFX3 motifs with Rfx3/Rfx7 in L2/3) and inverse correlations (FOXP motifs enriched in upper layers while Foxp2 expressed in L6, CUX motifs inversely correlated with Cux1/Cux2 expression).
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58, C60 integrate motif enrichment with gene expression data. The positive correlations support activator functions while inverse correlations are consistent with repressor functions (supported by literature citations C59, C60). The integration of multiple data types strengthens the conclusions, though the correlations are observational and do not prove direct regulatory relationships.

results.result: TF footprinting analysis showed layer-specific accessibility patterns: FOXP motifs most accessible in L2/3, L4, and L5 with least accessibility in L6; NEUROD motifs significantly more accessible in L4; and RFX motifs showing most accessibility in L2/3.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 describe TF footprinting results that provide single-base-pair resolution validation of motif accessibility patterns. The patterns are consistent with motif enrichment (C51-C54) and gene expression data (C55-C60), providing convergent evidence. Footprinting is a standard validation approach for ATAC-seq data.

results.result: Integration of chromatin accessibility, transcriptomic profiles, and TF binding motifs enabled construction of a regulatory network identifying Cux1/2, Foxp2, Nfia, Pou3f2, and Rorb as potential key layer-specific regulators. The network shows Foxp2 as central to upper/lower division targeting upper-layer TFs, CUX1 as a repressor of lower-layer TFs, and Tbr1/Nfia as activators of lower-layer TFs.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C64, C70, C76, C86 describe the main regulatory network. While the integration approach is sound and the network is based on multiple data types (accessibility, expression, motifs), the conclusions are largely inferential. The network represents putative interactions based on correlations and motif presence, not direct experimental validation of regulatory relationships. The use of terms like 'potential' and 'may' appropriately reflects this uncertainty. Functional validation experiments would be needed to confirm these regulatory interactions.

results.result: Nfia is expressed almost exclusively in L6 cells. Analysis of 55 Nfia-associated peaks identified 14 that were significantly more accessible (>2-fold, p<0.01) in L6 versus L4, located near an L6-specific TSS and downstream sites, containing accessible TBR, NFIA, and RFX motifs in L6 but not L4.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C101 provide detailed analysis of Nfia regulatory elements. The layer-specific expression is clearly demonstrated, differential accessibility is quantified with statistical thresholds, and specific motifs are identified. This represents a well-supported example of layer-specific gene regulation, though the functional significance of these elements would require experimental validation.

results.result: Cux1 is strongly expressed in upper but not lower cortical layers. Of 18 Cux1-associated peaks, 5 were differentially accessible (p<0.01, all more accessible in L4), located distal to TSS near the second exon. The TSS is accessible across all cell types, suggesting it is poised for transcription but expression requires distal enhancers containing NEUROD, FOS, EGR, FOXP, MEF2, and MEIS motifs.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C111 provide detailed analysis of Cux1 regulatory elements. The distinction between accessible TSS (poised) and layer-specific distal enhancers is well-supported by the data and represents an important mechanistic insight. The identification of specific motifs in the enhancers is consistent with the broader network model. However, the inference about TSS 'poising' versus enhancer-driven expression (C107) requires functional validation.

results.result: The FOXP motif near Cux1 may recruit FOXP2 and NuRD complexes to repress Cux1 transcription in lower layers, while EGR1/EGR3, MEF2C, and NEUROD may regulate expression in upper layers.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C113 propose specific regulatory mechanisms for Cux1. While the motif presence is documented (C111) and consistent with known FOXP2 function (C59, C67-C68), these are speculative mechanistic proposals based on correlative data. The use of 'may' appropriately indicates uncertainty. Direct experimental evidence (ChIP-seq, functional assays) would be needed to confirm these mechanisms.

results.result: A previously described developmental RORB-Pou3f2 regulatory interaction is not present in adult cortex: RORB binding sites near Pou3f2 show very little chromatin accessibility in adult cells, and Rorb and Pou3f2 are co-expressed in adult L2/3 and L4 cells, suggesting the chromatin state prevents this interaction after differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C134 identify an important developmental versus adult difference. The lack of accessibility at known RORB binding sites (C133) combined with co-expression of both genes in adult (C132) provides strong evidence that this developmental regulatory interaction is not maintained in adult cortex. This demonstrates context-dependent regulation and highlights the importance of studying adult tissue.

results.result: A previously reported POU3F2-Foxp2 interaction through a conserved binding site is not observed in adult visual cortex: the chromatin is inaccessible near the POU3F2 motif in Foxp2, and Foxp2 is not expressed in cell classes expressing Pou3f2 (layers 2-5).
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C139 identify another developmental/adult or tissue-specific difference. The inaccessibility of the conserved POU3F2 motif (C137) and mutually exclusive expression patterns (C139) provide strong evidence against this interaction in adult visual cortex, though it may occur in development or other tissues. This emphasizes context-dependent regulation.

results.result: Network analysis suggests FOXP2 may repress Mef2c in lower layers of adult visual cortex, but FOXP motifs near Mef2c exon 3 (identified in striatum) show only modest, non-significant decreased accessibility in lower cortical layers. Two peaks upstream of Mef2c TSS are less accessible in L6, suggesting FOXP2 may regulate Mef2c through different sites in cortex versus striatum.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C144 propose tissue-specific regulatory mechanisms. While the network analysis suggests FOXP2-Mef2c interaction (C141), the lack of significant accessibility changes at striatum-identified sites (C142) and identification of alternative upstream sites (C143) is appropriately cautious. The hypothesis of tissue-specific binding sites (C144) is plausible but speculative, requiring experimental validation through tissue-specific ChIP-seq or functional assays.

results.result: The study provides chromatin accessibility data at layer-specific cell class resolution, enabling identification of unique accessible sites for each layer and layer-wide patterns of TF accessibility. Integration of accessibility, gene expression, and motif data identified interactions that may drive expression of key regulators Nfia and Cux1.
results.evaluation: Claims C115, C117, C153-C155 summarize the study's contributions. The layer-specific resolution is clearly demonstrated (vs. previous whole-brain or pan-cortical studies, C116), and the integrative analysis approach is well-executed. The identification of putative regulatory interactions for Nfia and Cux1 is supported by detailed analysis (C97-C113), though the mechanistic claims remain inferential.

results.result: Distinct transcription factor families for L5 were not clearly identified, possibly due to heterogeneity of cell types in the Rbp4-Cre line, which labels at least nine transcriptomic cell types including L5a and L5b subtypes with different characteristics.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C120 acknowledge an important limitation. The failure to identify L5-specific TF families is honestly reported (C118), and the proposed explanation based on known cell type heterogeneity (C120, citing Tasic et al., 2016) is reasonable. This demonstrates appropriate scientific rigor in acknowledging limitations and their likely causes.

results.result: Comparisons between adult and developmental data emphasize the importance of developmental, anatomical, and cell type context in chromatin accessibility and transcriptomic regulation studies. Some TF target sites from development may be retained in adulthood while others may differ due to accessibility changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C147 draw appropriate general conclusions from the developmental versus adult comparisons (C131-C139). The emphasis on context-dependence is well-supported by the specific examples provided. The speculation about retention versus change of target sites (C147) is appropriately cautious and highlights the need for developmental studies.
